title: Algorithms
intro: One card per trick: a tiny problem, the words that signal it, and a short tested template. Start with [Recognize the pattern](#algo-recognize).

sections.title: Recognize the pattern
sections.summary: Which trick does this problem need? Map its words to a pattern.
sections.body:
**Problem:** the exam never tells you the pattern. Choosing it is half the work.

**How to approach any problem:**

1. Restate it and solve one tiny example by hand.
2. Read the constraints: n tells you the cost you can afford ([Big-O](#algo-big-o)).
3. Match the words in the problem to a row of the table below.
4. Say the brute force and its cost, then code the trick from its card.
5. Test the tiny example and edge cases (empty, one item, duplicates), then state time and space.

| Signal in the problem | Trick | Card |
|---|---|---|
| constraints line, `n <= 10^5` | pick the cost that fits n | [Big-O and input size](#algo-big-o) |
| "one pass", "best so far", "O(1) space" | running state | [Arrays and strings (one pass)](#algo-arrays-strings) |
| "unsorted" + "pair", "duplicate", "count", "group by" | dict or set | [Hashing (dict and set)](#algo-hashing) |
| "sorted" + "pair or triplet", "palindrome", "in place" | two pointers | [Two pointers](#algo-two-pointers) |
| "contiguous", "longest or shortest substring", "at most k" | sliding window | [Sliding window](#algo-sliding-window) |
| "valid parentheses", "nested", "undo" | stack | [Stack](#algo-stack) |
| "next greater or smaller", "max of every window" | monotonic stack or deque | [Monotonic stack](#algo-monotonic-stack) |
| "sorted" + "find", "O(log n)", "minimum speed such that" | binary search (on the answer) | [Binary search](#algo-binary-search) |
| "intervals", "meetings", "merge overlapping" | sort by start, scan | [Sorting and intervals](#algo-sorting-intervals) |
| "fewest to remove", "max non-overlapping", "can you reach" | greedy (sort by end) | [Greedy](#algo-greedy) |
| "range sum" many times, "subarray sum equals k" | prefix sum + dict | [Prefix sum](#algo-prefix-sum) |
| "k-th largest", "top k", "merge k sorted", "median stream" | heap | [Heap (priority queue)](#algo-heap) |
| "linked list", "cycle", "middle", "reverse" | pointer rewiring, fast and slow | [Linked lists](#algo-linked-list) |
| "binary tree", "depth", "path", "level by level" | DFS recursion or BFS levels | [Binary trees (DFS and BFS)](#algo-trees) |
| "binary search tree", "k-th smallest", "valid BST" | in-order traversal, ranges | [Binary search trees](#algo-bst) |
| "islands", "connected", "minimum steps" | BFS or DFS with a seen set | [Graphs: BFS and DFS](#algo-graphs-bfs-dfs) |
| "board", "spiral", "rotate", "each turn" | direction arrays, copy for updates | [Grid simulation](#algo-grid-simulation) |
| "prerequisites", "dependencies", "order" | count incoming edges (Kahn) | [Topological sort](#algo-topological-sort) |
| "same group?", "provinces", "redundant edge" | union-find | [Union-find](#algo-union-find) |
| "weighted", "minimum cost", "within k stops" | Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford | [Shortest paths (Dijkstra)](#algo-shortest-path) |
| "all", "generate every", "permutations", small n | choose, recurse, undo | [Backtracking](#algo-backtracking) |
| "number of ways", "min or max to reach", repeated sub-questions | dp over one index | [Dynamic programming 1D](#algo-dp-1d) |
| "two strings", "edit distance", "grid paths" | dp table over two indices | [Dynamic programming 2D](#algo-dp-2d) |
| "design a class", "O(1) get and put" | dict + an ordered structure | [Data structure design](#algo-design) |
| "log", "events per user", "session", "no pandas" | group, sort, scan | [Data processing in plain Python](#algo-data-processing) |

**Next:** check how big the input is before choosing -> [Big-O and input size](#algo-big-o)

sections.title: Big-O and input size
sections.summary: Will my solution be fast enough for this input size?
sections.body:
**Problem:** 100,000 numbers, is there a duplicate? Comparing every pair is about 5,000,000,000 checks (too slow). A set needs 100,000 steps (instant).

**Signal:** the constraints line, e.g. `n <= 10^5`. Python does roughly 10 million simple steps per second.

**Trick:** Read n first and pick the cost that fits: `n <= 20` -> `2^n` is fine, `n <= 500` -> `n^3`, `n <= 5,000` -> `n^2`, `n <= 10^6` -> `n log n` or `n`.

```python
def has_dup_slow(a):            # O(n^2): compares every pair
    return any(a[i] == a[j] for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i))
def has_dup(a):                 # O(n): a set lookup is O(1)
    seen = set()
    for x in a:
        if x in seen: return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False
```

**Cost:** hidden costs in Python: `x in list` is O(n) but `x in set` is O(1); `list.pop(0)` is O(n) (use `deque.popleft()`); `sorted` is O(n log n); `s += ch` in a loop can be O(n^2) (collect in a list, then `''.join`).

**Practice:** [217. Contains Duplicate](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate/), [1. Two Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/)

**Next:** Find the best day to buy and the best day to sell a stock, in one pass -> [Arrays and strings](#algo-arrays-strings)

sections.title: Arrays and strings (one pass)
sections.summary: Answer in one pass over the array with a small running state.
sections.body:
**Problem:** prices `[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]` -> `5` (buy at 1, sell at 6).

**Signal:** "one pass", "in place", "O(1) extra space", "best so far", "maximum profit".

**Trick:** Walk once and keep a tiny running state (smallest so far, best so far). Build strings in a list and `''.join` at the end.

```python
def max_profit(prices):
    low, best = float("inf"), 0         # cheapest so far, best profit so far
    for p in prices:
        low = min(low, p)
        best = max(best, p - low)
    return best
```

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Practice:** [121. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock](https://leetcode.com/problems/best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock/), [31. Next Permutation](https://leetcode.com/problems/next-permutation/)

**Next:** Find two numbers that add up to 9 in an unsorted list -> [Hashing](#algo-hashing)

sections.title: Hashing (dict and set)
sections.summary: Find something by its value instantly.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]`, target 9 -> `[0, 1]` (2 + 7). Words `eat, tea, tan, nat, bat` -> groups `[eat, tea], [tan, nat], [bat]`.

**Signal:** "unsorted", "pair that sums to", "seen before", "duplicate", "count how often", "group by", "anagram".

**Trick:** Store what you have seen in a dict (value -> index or count). For each x, ask "is `target - x` already there?" To group, use a key that is the same for the whole group (sorted letters).

```python
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                           # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen: return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
from collections import defaultdict
def group_anagrams(words):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words: g["".join(sorted(w))].append(w)
    return list(g.values())
```

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(n) space. `Counter(a)` counts everything in one line.

**Practice:** [1. Two Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/), [49. Group Anagrams](https://leetcode.com/problems/group-anagrams/), [128. Longest Consecutive Sequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-consecutive-sequence/)

**Next:** Same pair question, but the array is sorted and you may use no extra memory -> [Two pointers](#algo-two-pointers)

sections.title: Two pointers
sections.summary: Find a pair in a sorted array without extra memory.
sections.body:
**Problem:** sorted `[1, 2, 4, 7, 11]`, target 9 -> indices `(1, 3)` (2 + 7).

**Signal:** "sorted array" + "pair" or "triplet", "palindrome", "in place", "move zeroes", "container with most water".

**Trick:** One pointer at each end. Sum too small: move the left one right. Too big: move the right one left. Each step removes one candidate for good.

```python
def pair_with_sum(a, target):           # a is sorted
    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
    while i < j:
        s = a[i] + a[j]
        if s == target: return i, j
        if s < target: i += 1           # need bigger
        else: j -= 1                    # need smaller
    return None
```

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(1) space (plus O(n log n) if you must sort first). 3Sum = fix one number, then two pointers on the rest: O(n^2).

**Practice:** [125. Valid Palindrome](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-palindrome/), [15. 3Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/3sum/), [11. Container With Most Water](https://leetcode.com/problems/container-with-most-water/)

**Next:** Longest piece of a string with no repeated letter -> [Sliding window](#algo-sliding-window)

sections.title: Sliding window
sections.summary: Best contiguous piece of an array or string.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `"abcabcbb"` -> `3` (`"abc"`).

**Signal:** "contiguous", "subarray" or "substring", "longest" or "shortest", "at most k", "window of size k".

**Trick:** Grow the right end one step at a time. While the window breaks the rule, shrink it from the left. Record the best window after each step.

```python
from collections import Counter
def longest_unique(s):
    count, left, best = Counter(), 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] += 1                  # grow: add s[right]
        while count[ch] > 1:            # rule broken: shrink from the left
            count[s[left]] -= 1; left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

**Cost:** O(n) time (each item enters and leaves once), O(size of alphabet) space.

**Practice:** [3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/), [424. Longest Repeating Character Replacement](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-repeating-character-replacement/), [76. Minimum Window Substring](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-window-substring/)

**Next:** Is `"([)]"` correctly nested? -> [Stack](#algo-stack)

sections.title: Stack
sections.summary: Match the most recent open thing.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `"([]{})"` -> `True`, `"([)]"` -> `False`.

**Signal:** "valid parentheses", "nested", "matching", "undo", "most recent", "evaluate expression".

**Trick:** Push every opener. On a closer, the top of the stack must be its partner. At the end the stack must be empty.

```python
def is_valid(s):
    pair, stack = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}, []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in pair:
            if not stack or stack.pop() != pair[ch]: return False
        else: stack.append(ch)
    return not stack
```

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(n) space. A Python list is the stack: `append` and `pop`.

**Practice:** [20. Valid Parentheses](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-parentheses/), [155. Min Stack](https://leetcode.com/problems/min-stack/), [150. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation](https://leetcode.com/problems/evaluate-reverse-polish-notation/)

**Next:** For each day, how many days until a warmer one? -> [Monotonic stack](#algo-monotonic-stack)

sections.title: Monotonic stack
sections.summary: Next bigger (or smaller) item for every position.
sections.body:
**Problem:** temperatures `[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]` -> `[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]`.

**Signal:** "next greater" or "next smaller", "days until warmer", "largest rectangle", "maximum of every window".

**Trick:** Keep a stack of indices still waiting for an answer, values going down. A bigger value pops them and answers them. For the max of every window, use a deque the same way.

```python
def days_until_warmer(t):
    ans, stack = [0] * len(t), []       # stack: waiting indices, temps going down
    for i, x in enumerate(t):
        while stack and t[stack[-1]] < x:
            j = stack.pop(); ans[j] = i - j
        stack.append(i)
    return ans
```

**Cost:** O(n) time (each index is pushed and popped once), O(n) space.

**Practice:** [739. Daily Temperatures](https://leetcode.com/problems/daily-temperatures/), [84. Largest Rectangle in Histogram](https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-rectangle-in-histogram/), [239. Sliding Window Maximum](https://leetcode.com/problems/sliding-window-maximum/)

**Next:** Find 7 in a sorted list of 1,000,000 numbers in about 20 steps -> [Binary search](#algo-binary-search)

sections.title: Binary search
sections.summary: Find a position or the smallest value that works, halving each step.
sections.body:
**Problem:** sorted `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]`, find 7 -> index `3`. Koko: piles `[3, 6, 7, 11]`, 8 hours -> slowest speed `4`.

**Signal:** "sorted", "O(log n)", "first or last position", "insert position", "minimum speed or capacity such that" (search on the answer).

**Trick:** Keep a range `[lo, hi]`, look at the middle, throw away the half that cannot hold the answer. For "smallest x that works", write a yes/no check `ok(x)` and search on x.

```python
def first_true(lo, hi, ok):             # smallest x in [lo, hi] with ok(x) True
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid): hi = mid
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo
# a = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]: first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: i == len(a) or a[i] >= 7) -> 3
# Koko: first_true(1, max(piles), lambda k: sum(ceil(p / k) for p in piles) <= h) -> 4
```

**Cost:** O(log n) steps; search on the answer costs O(log(range) x cost of ok). `bisect.bisect_left(a, x)` does the sorted-array case.

**Practice:** [704. Binary Search](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-search/), [33. Search in Rotated Sorted Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/search-in-rotated-sorted-array/), [875. Koko Eating Bananas](https://leetcode.com/problems/koko-eating-bananas/)

**Next:** Meetings `[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10]` overlap: merge them -> [Sorting and intervals](#algo-sorting-intervals)

sections.title: Sorting and intervals
sections.summary: Merge or compare ranges after sorting them.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `[[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]` -> `[[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]`.

**Signal:** "intervals", "meetings", "overlapping", "merge", "schedule", "ordered by position or time".

**Trick:** Sort by start. Compare each interval with the last merged one: if it starts before that one ends, extend the end; otherwise start a new one.

```python
def merge(intervals):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(intervals):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]: out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else: out.append([s, e])
    return out
```

**Cost:** O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) space.

**Practice:** [56. Merge Intervals](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-intervals/), [853. Car Fleet](https://leetcode.com/problems/car-fleet/), [57. Insert Interval](https://leetcode.com/problems/insert-interval/)

**Next:** Remove the fewest meetings so that none overlap -> [Greedy](#algo-greedy)

sections.title: Greedy
sections.summary: Take the best-looking choice at each step, when that is provably safe.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `[[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 3]]` -> remove `1` interval (`[1, 3]`).

**Signal:** "minimum number to remove or add", "maximum number of non-overlapping", "can you reach the end", "partition into as many parts as possible".

**Trick:** Sort, then always take the choice that leaves the most room (here: the meeting that ends first). Before trusting it, try to break it with a tiny counterexample; if you can, use DP.

```python
def min_remove(intervals):              # fewest to drop so none overlap
    end, removed = float("-inf"), 0
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: x[1]):   # earliest end first
        if s >= end: end = e            # fits: keep it
        else: removed += 1              # overlaps the kept one: drop it
    return removed
```

**Cost:** O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

**Practice:** [435. Non-overlapping Intervals](https://leetcode.com/problems/non-overlapping-intervals/), [763. Partition Labels](https://leetcode.com/problems/partition-labels/), [621. Task Scheduler](https://leetcode.com/problems/task-scheduler/)

**Next:** Answer many questions like "sum of items 1 to 4?" fast -> [Prefix sum](#algo-prefix-sum)

sections.title: Prefix sum
sections.summary: Any range sum in one subtraction; count subarrays with a given sum.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]`, sum of `a[1..4]` -> `11`. How many subarrays of `[1, 1, 1]` sum to 2 -> `2`.

**Signal:** "sum of range i to j" asked many times, "subarray sum equals k", "count subarrays", "product of array except self".

**Trick:** `P[i]` = sum of the first i items, so `sum a[i..j] = P[j+1] - P[i]`. To count subarrays summing to k, keep a dict of prefix sums seen and look up `cur - k`.

```python
from itertools import accumulate
P = [0] + list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]))   # P[5] - P[1] = 11
def count_subarrays(a, k):              # how many subarrays sum to k
    seen, cur, count = {0: 1}, 0, 0     # prefix sum -> how often seen
    for x in a:
        cur += x
        count += seen.get(cur - k, 0)
        seen[cur] = seen.get(cur, 0) + 1
    return count
```

**Cost:** O(n) to build, then O(1) per range question; O(n) space.

**Practice:** [303. Range Sum Query - Immutable](https://leetcode.com/problems/range-sum-query-immutable/), [560. Subarray Sum Equals K](https://leetcode.com/problems/subarray-sum-equals-k/), [238. Product of Array Except Self](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/)

**Next:** Numbers keep arriving: always know the 3rd largest -> [Heap](#algo-heap)

sections.title: Heap (priority queue)
sections.summary: Always get the smallest or largest item fast.
sections.body:
**Problem:** stream `4, 5, 8, 2, 3`, k = 3 -> 3rd largest is `4`. `[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]`, top 2 frequent -> `[1, 2]`.

**Signal:** "k-th largest or smallest", "top k", "k closest", "merge k sorted", "median of a stream", "always process the cheapest next".

**Trick:** `heapq` is a min-heap: `h[0]` is the smallest. Keep a heap of size k: push, and pop when it grows past k; then `h[0]` is the k-th largest. For a max-heap, push `-x`.

```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter
def kth_largest(nums, k):               # heap holds the k largest so far
    h = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)
    return h[0]
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    return [x for x, _ in Counter(nums).most_common(k)]
```

**Cost:** O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Push and pop are O(log n); peek is O(1).

**Practice:** [703. Kth Largest Element in a Stream](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-a-stream/), [347. Top K Frequent Elements](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/), [23. Merge k Sorted Lists](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-k-sorted-lists/)

**Next:** Reverse `1 -> 2 -> 3` without building a new list -> [Linked lists](#algo-linked-list)

sections.title: Linked lists
sections.summary: Rewire pointers in place; fast and slow pointers.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `1 -> 2 -> 3` -> `3 -> 2 -> 1`. A list whose tail points back into it -> has a cycle: `True`.

**Signal:** "linked list", "in place", "reverse", "cycle", "middle node", "k-th from the end", "merge two sorted lists".

**Trick:** Change one `next` pointer at a time while holding `prev`. Fast pointer moves 2, slow moves 1: they meet if there is a cycle; when fast ends, slow is at the middle. A dummy head makes merging easy.

```python
def reverse(head, prev=None):           # 1->2->3 becomes 3->2->1
    while head:
        head.next, prev, head = prev, head, head.next
    return prev
def has_cycle(head):                    # fast moves 2, slow moves 1
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast: return True
    return False
```

**Cost:** O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Practice:** [206. Reverse Linked List](https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-linked-list/), [21. Merge Two Sorted Lists](https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-two-sorted-lists/), [141. Linked List Cycle](https://leetcode.com/problems/linked-list-cycle/)

**Next:** How deep is this tree? -> [Binary trees](#algo-trees)

sections.title: Binary trees (DFS and BFS)
sections.summary: Solve a tree by combining the answers of its two subtrees, or level by level.
sections.body:
**Problem:** tree `3` with children `9` and `20`, and `20` has children `15, 7` -> depth `3`; levels `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`.

**Signal:** "binary tree", "depth" or "height", "path", "level by level", "right side view", "ancestor".

**Trick:** DFS: the answer for a node = combine the answers of its left and right child (recursion). BFS: keep the current level in a queue and build the next level from it.

```python
def max_depth(node):                    # DFS: combine the two children
    if not node: return 0
    return 1 + max(max_depth(node.left), max_depth(node.right))
def levels(root):                       # BFS: one level per round
    out, level = [], [root] if root else []
    while level:
        out.append([n.val for n in level])
        level = [c for n in level for c in (n.left, n.right) if c]
    return out
```

**Cost:** O(n) time; O(height) space for DFS, O(widest level) for BFS.

**Practice:** [104. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-depth-of-binary-tree/), [102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal](https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-level-order-traversal/), [236. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-tree/)

**Next:** Every left child is smaller and every right child is bigger: is the tree valid, and what is the 3rd smallest? -> [Binary search trees](#algo-bst)

sections.title: Binary search trees
sections.summary: Use the order rule: left < node < right.
sections.body:
**Problem:** BST `5` (left `3` with children `2, 4`; right `7`) -> in order `[2, 3, 4, 5, 7]`, 3rd smallest `4`. Put `6` under `3` -> not valid.

**Signal:** "binary search tree", "valid BST", "k-th smallest", "in sorted order", "closest value".

**Trick:** In-order (left, node, right) visits the values sorted. To validate, pass the allowed range `(lo, hi)` down: a node only checking its own children is not enough.

```python
def is_bst(node, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    if not node: return True
    if not lo < node.val < hi: return False
    return is_bst(node.left, lo, node.val) and is_bst(node.right, node.val, hi)
def inorder(node):                      # yields the values in sorted order
    if node:
        yield from inorder(node.left); yield node.val; yield from inorder(node.right)
# k-th smallest: next(itertools.islice(inorder(root), k - 1, None))
```

**Cost:** O(n) to visit all; O(height) for one search; O(height) space.

**Practice:** [98. Validate Binary Search Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/validate-binary-search-tree/), [230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst/), [235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-search-tree/)

**Next:** Count the islands of 1s in a grid -> [Graphs: BFS and DFS](#algo-graphs-bfs-dfs)

sections.title: Graphs: BFS and DFS
sections.summary: Explore connected things; fewest steps when every step costs the same.
sections.body:
**Problem:** grid `11000 / 11000 / 00100 / 00011` -> `3` islands. From the top-left of `111 / 011 / 001` to the bottom-right -> `4` steps.

**Signal:** "connected", "islands", "regions", "can you reach", "minimum number of steps or moves" (BFS), "spreads every minute" (BFS from all sources at once).

**Trick:** Visit each cell once with a `seen` set. Islands: start a search from every unseen `1` and count the starts. Fewest steps: BFS with a queue, starting from all sources together.

```python
from collections import deque
def bfs(grid, starts):                  # steps from the nearest start to each reachable '1'
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0]); dist = {s: 0 for s in starts}; q = deque(starts)
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and grid[nr][nc] == "1" and (nr, nc) not in dist:
                dist[(nr, nc)] = dist[(r, c)] + 1; q.append((nr, nc))
    return dist
```

**Cost:** O(V + E) time; for a grid O(rows x cols). O(V) space.

**Practice:** [200. Number of Islands](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-islands/), [994. Rotting Oranges](https://leetcode.com/problems/rotting-oranges/), [127. Word Ladder](https://leetcode.com/problems/word-ladder/)

**Next:** A robot walks on a board and turns by fixed rules -> [Grid simulation](#algo-grid-simulation)

sections.title: Grid simulation
sections.summary: Follow movement rules on a 2D board exactly.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]` read in a spiral -> `[1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 8, 7, 4, 5]`.

**Signal:** "matrix" or "board", "spiral", "rotate", "move in a direction", "each turn", "all cells change at the same time".

**Trick:** Direction arrays `dr, dc`; turn right = `(d + 1) % 4`; check bounds before moving. Rotate 90 degrees clockwise: `list(zip(*m[::-1]))`. Simultaneous updates: write into a copy.

```python
def spiral(m):
    R, C = len(m), len(m[0]); dr, dc = (0, 1, 0, -1), (1, 0, -1, 0)
    r = c = d = 0; seen, out = set(), []
    for _ in range(R * C):
        out.append(m[r][c]); seen.add((r, c))
        nr, nc = r + dr[d], c + dc[d]
        if not (0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C) or (nr, nc) in seen:
            d = (d + 1) % 4; nr, nc = r + dr[d], c + dc[d]
        r, c = nr, nc
    return out
```

**Cost:** O(rows x cols) time and space.

**Practice:** [54. Spiral Matrix](https://leetcode.com/problems/spiral-matrix/), [48. Rotate Image](https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-image/), [289. Game of Life](https://leetcode.com/problems/game-of-life/)

**Next:** Course 0 must come before 1 and 2, and both before 3: in what order can you take them? -> [Topological sort](#algo-topological-sort)

sections.title: Topological sort
sections.summary: Order tasks so every dependency comes first; detect a cycle.
sections.body:
**Problem:** 4 courses, prerequisites `[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]` -> order `[0, 1, 2, 3]`. `[1, 0], [0, 1]` -> `[]` (a cycle, impossible).

**Signal:** "prerequisites", "dependencies", "must come before", "build order", "is it possible to finish all".

**Trick:** Count incoming edges per node. Start with the nodes that have 0, remove them, and lower their neighbors' counts. If some nodes never reach 0, there is a cycle.

```python
def topo_order(n, prereqs):             # [a, b] means b before a
    graph, indeg = [[] for _ in range(n)], [0] * n
    for a, b in prereqs: graph[b].append(a); indeg[a] += 1
    order = [i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0]
    for u in order:                     # order grows while we loop
        for v in graph[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0: order.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []   # [] means a cycle
```

**Cost:** O(V + E) time and space.

**Practice:** [207. Course Schedule](https://leetcode.com/problems/course-schedule/), [210. Course Schedule II](https://leetcode.com/problems/course-schedule-ii/)

**Next:** Friends of friends form groups: how many separate groups? -> [Union-find](#algo-union-find)

sections.title: Union-find
sections.summary: Merge groups and ask "same group?" almost instantly.
sections.body:
**Problem:** 5 people, friendships `(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4)` -> `2` groups.

**Signal:** "connected components" with edges arriving one by one, "same group?", "number of provinces", "redundant connection", "merge accounts".

**Trick:** Each node points to a parent; the root names the group. `find` walks up to the root (and shortens the path). `union` points one root at the other.

```python
def count_groups(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]   # shorten the path
        return x
    for a, b in edges:
        parent[find(a)] = find(b)                          # union
    return sum(find(i) == i for i in range(n))
```

**Cost:** almost O(1) per operation, O(n) space. If `find(a) == find(b)` before a union, that edge is redundant.

**Practice:** [547. Number of Provinces](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-provinces/), [684. Redundant Connection](https://leetcode.com/problems/redundant-connection/), [721. Accounts Merge](https://leetcode.com/problems/accounts-merge/)

**Next:** Roads have different lengths: what is the shortest travel time? -> [Shortest paths](#algo-shortest-path)

sections.title: Shortest paths (Dijkstra)
sections.summary: Cheapest route when edges have different costs.
sections.body:
**Problem:** A -> B costs 1, B -> C costs 2, A -> C costs 5. Cheapest A to C -> `3` (through B), not 5.

**Signal:** "weighted", "minimum cost or time", "network delay", "cheapest", "within k stops" (Bellman-Ford), "all pairs" (Floyd-Warshall).

**Trick:** Dijkstra: a heap of `(distance, node)`; pop the closest node, try to improve its neighbors, skip old heap entries. Costs must not be negative. At most k edges: Bellman-Ford, k + 1 rounds over all edges, using a copy each round.

```python
import heapq
def dijkstra(graph, src):               # graph[u] = [(v, cost), ...], cost >= 0
    dist, heap = {src: 0}, [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]: continue        # old entry
        for v, w in graph.get(u, []):
            if d + w < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                dist[v] = d + w; heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, v))
    return dist
```

**Cost:** Dijkstra O(E log V); Bellman-Ford O(k x E); Floyd-Warshall O(V^3).

**Practice:** [743. Network Delay Time](https://leetcode.com/problems/network-delay-time/), [787. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops](https://leetcode.com/problems/cheapest-flights-within-k-stops/), [1631. Path With Minimum Effort](https://leetcode.com/problems/path-with-minimum-effort/)

**Next:** List every subset of `[1, 2, 3]` -> [Backtracking](#algo-backtracking)

sections.title: Backtracking
sections.summary: Generate every candidate; undo and prune.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `[1, 2, 3]` -> all `8` subsets: `[], [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3]`.

**Signal:** "all", "every", "generate", "subsets", "combinations", "permutations", "place N queens", "word search", and a small n (about 20 or less).

**Trick:** Choose, go deeper, undo the choice. Stop a branch early (prune) as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer.

```python
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums): out.append(path[:]); return
        path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()   # take nums[i], then undo
        go(i + 1)                                     # skip nums[i]
    go(0)
    return out
```

**Cost:** O(2^n x n) for subsets, O(n! x n) for permutations; O(n) recursion depth.

**Practice:** [78. Subsets](https://leetcode.com/problems/subsets/), [39. Combination Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/combination-sum/), [79. Word Search](https://leetcode.com/problems/word-search/)

**Next:** Count the ways to climb 5 stairs, 1 or 2 steps at a time, without listing them all -> [Dynamic programming 1D](#algo-dp-1d)

sections.title: Dynamic programming 1D
sections.summary: Best value or number of ways when the same sub-question repeats.
sections.body:
**Problem:** climb 5 stairs, 1 or 2 steps -> `8` ways. Rob houses `[2, 7, 9, 3, 1]`, never two neighbors -> `12` (2 + 9 + 1). Coins `[1, 2, 5]`, amount 11 -> `3` coins.

**Signal:** "number of ways", "minimum or maximum to reach", "can you make", choices at each step, and plain recursion repeats the same work.

**Trick:** Define `dp[i]` = the answer for the first i items. Write `dp[i]` from earlier values (`dp[i-1]`, `dp[i-2]`). Keep only the values you still need.

```python
def rob(a):                             # dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i])
    prev, cur = 0, 0
    for x in a:
        prev, cur = cur, max(cur, prev + x)
    return cur
def coin_change(coins, amount):         # dp[s] = fewest coins that make s
    dp = [0] + [float("inf")] * amount
    for s in range(1, amount + 1):
        dp[s] = min([dp[s - c] + 1 for c in coins if c <= s] + [dp[s]])
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] < float("inf") else -1
```

**Cost:** O(n) for robber, O(amount x coins) for coins; O(1) or O(amount) space.

**Practice:** [70. Climbing Stairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/climbing-stairs/), [198. House Robber](https://leetcode.com/problems/house-robber/), [322. Coin Change](https://leetcode.com/problems/coin-change/)

**Next:** How alike are two strings, `"abcde"` and `"ace"`? -> [Dynamic programming 2D](#algo-dp-2d)

sections.title: Dynamic programming 2D
sections.summary: Two indices in the state: two strings or a grid.
sections.body:
**Problem:** `"abcde"` and `"ace"` -> longest common subsequence `3` (`"ace"`).

**Signal:** "two strings", "common subsequence", "edit distance", "paths in a grid", "substring from i to j", "knapsack with capacity".

**Trick:** `dp[i][j]` = answer for the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b. Letters match: diagonal + 1. Otherwise: the better of up or left.

```python
def lcs(a, b):                          # dp[i][j]: LCS of a[:i] and b[:j]
    dp = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i in range(1, len(a) + 1):
        for j in range(1, len(b) + 1):
            if a[i-1] == b[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
            else: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
    return dp[-1][-1]
```

**Cost:** O(m x n) time and space; keep only two rows for O(n) space.

**Practice:** [1143. Longest Common Subsequence](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-common-subsequence/), [62. Unique Paths](https://leetcode.com/problems/unique-paths/), [72. Edit Distance](https://leetcode.com/problems/edit-distance/)

**Next:** Build a cache that forgets the least recently used item, with O(1) get and put -> [Data structure design](#algo-design)

sections.title: Data structure design
sections.summary: Build a class whose operations meet given time limits.
sections.body:
**Problem:** LRU cache of size 2: `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`, `get(1)` -> `1`, `put(3, 3)` drops key 2, `get(2)` -> `-1`.

**Signal:** "design a class", "implement", "each operation in O(1)", "get and put", "LRU", "time-based", "min stack".

**Trick:** Combine two structures: a dict for O(1) lookup plus something that keeps order (OrderedDict, deque, heap, or a sorted list with `bisect`).

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, cap): self.cap, self.d = cap, OrderedDict()
    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.d: return -1
        self.d.move_to_end(k); return self.d[k]      # mark as most recent
    def put(self, k, v):
        self.d[k] = v; self.d.move_to_end(k)
        if len(self.d) > self.cap: self.d.popitem(last=False)   # drop the oldest
```

**Cost:** O(1) per get and put, O(capacity) space.

**Practice:** [146. LRU Cache](https://leetcode.com/problems/lru-cache/), [155. Min Stack](https://leetcode.com/problems/min-stack/), [981. Time Based Key-Value Store](https://leetcode.com/problems/time-based-key-value-store/)

**Next:** A raw click log: split each user's clicks into sessions -> [Data processing](#algo-data-processing)

sections.title: Data processing in plain Python
sections.summary: Group, sort and scan event logs without pandas.
sections.body:
**Problem:** clicks `(u1, 0), (u2, 5), (u1, 50), (u1, 10)`, new session after a gap over 30 -> `{u1: 2, u2: 1}`.

**Signal:** "log", "events", "per user", "session", "timestamps", "top creators", "without pandas".

**Trick:** Group with `defaultdict(list)`, sort each group by time, scan once with a running state. Top k: `Counter(...).most_common(k)`.

```python
from collections import defaultdict
def sessions(events, gap=30):           # events: (user, time)
    by_user = defaultdict(list)
    for u, t in events: by_user[u].append(t)
    out = {}
    for u, ts in by_user.items():
        ts.sort()
        out[u] = 1 + sum(b - a > gap for a, b in zip(ts, ts[1:]))
    return out
```

**Cost:** O(n log n) for the sorts, O(n) space.

**Practice:** [811. Subdomain Visit Count](https://leetcode.com/problems/subdomain-visit-count/), [692. Top K Frequent Words](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-words/), [1604. Alert Using Same Key-Card Three or More Times in a One Hour Period](https://leetcode.com/problems/alert-using-same-key-card-three-or-more-times-in-a-one-hour-period/)
